ideas.title: Buy back time, not more things
ideas.idea:
Spending money to get time back may do more for your wellbeing than spending it on things.

Most of us feel short of time, yet reach for stuff when we have a spare few euro. In 2017 a team led by Ashley Whillans, with Elizabeth Dunn and colleagues, tested the alternative. They looked at what happens when people pay to shed a chore or a commute, such as a cleaner, a delivery, or an errand done by someone else. In a survey of more than 6,000 adults across four countries, those who spent money this way reported higher life satisfaction, and the link held at every income level. In a small field experiment, the same people felt happier after a time-saving purchase than after a material one.

The point is to notice that hours are scarcer than euro.
ideas.deep_dive:
The paper is "Buying time promotes happiness", published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2017 by Whillans, Dunn, Paul Smeets, Rene Bekkers and Michael Norton. It grew out of a plain observation: in rich countries, people report feeling more rushed than ever, and chronic time pressure is linked to lower wellbeing. Money is one of the few things that can be traded for time, yet most people do not do the trade.

The researchers combined two kinds of evidence. First, a survey of 6,271 adults in the United States, Canada, Denmark and the Netherlands asked how much they spent each month on services that free up time, and how satisfied they were with life. People who spent more on time-saving purchases were more satisfied, and the pattern was similar for richer and poorer respondents. Only around 28 per cent reported spending anything this way, averaging about $148 a month.

Second, the team ran an experiment, because a survey cannot say which causes which. Sixty working adults in Canada were given $40 on two weekends, once to spend on a time-saving purchase and once on a material one. They rated their mood afterwards on a five-point scale. Time-saving purchases scored about 4.0 against about 3.7, and people felt less time stress.

The limits are real. The experiment was small and the sum modest. The survey shows a link, not proof. And the idea is about discretionary spending: it does nothing for those who cannot afford the basics, and the effect may differ across tasks and people.

examples.title: Four countries, one pattern
examples.text: Whillans and colleagues surveyed 6,271 working adults in the United States, Canada, Denmark and the Netherlands. They asked about monthly spending on things that buy time, like paying someone to clean, cook or run errands. Those who did so reported greater life satisfaction, and the relationship held whether people earned a lot or a little. Only about 28 per cent reported any such spending, averaging roughly $148 a month. So the most common choice was to spend nothing on saving time at all, even among people who could afford it.

examples.title: The $40 weekend experiment
examples.text: To test cause and effect, the researchers recruited 60 working adults in Canada and gave each $40 on two separate weekends. On one, they had to spend it on a time-saving purchase, such as paying for a meal to be delivered or a task done for them. On the other, they bought a material item. Afterwards participants rated their happiness: about 4.0 out of 5 after the time-saving weekend, against about 3.7 after the material one. They also reported feeling less time pressure in the week they had bought time.

examples.title: What people say they would buy
examples.text: In a separate part of the study, 98 working adults were asked how they would spend an unexpected $40 windfall. Only 2 per cent of the purchases they described were time-saving ones. Most imagined spending it on goods or treats. Harvard Magazine's account of the work makes the same point from real life: people who outsource chores like housecleaning, or who live closer to work, tend to report being happier, yet the default for most of us is still to buy something we can hold.

why: Evidence: a survey of 6,271 adults in four countries plus a randomised experiment with 60 working adults in Canada, published in PNAS (2017).
Caveat: the experiment was small, the sum was only $40, and the survey shows a link rather than proof. It applies to people with spare money, not those struggling with basics.
ideas.try_this: What is one recurring chore you dislike that you could pay someone to do, or remove, for under €40 a month? Try it for four weeks and notice what you do with the time.

ideas.title: A rare coincidence isn't proof of guilt
ideas.idea:
"How unlikely is this by chance?" and "How likely is it that the accused is innocent?" are different questions, and mixing them up has put innocent people in prison.

This is the prosecutor's fallacy. Suppose an event is very rare if someone is innocent. It feels as though that makes innocence very unlikely too. It doesn't, because you have to compare it with the alternative explanation, which may be rarer still. Winning the lottery is a one-in-millions event, yet someone wins most weeks. A baby dying suddenly is rare; two such deaths in one family is rarer; but a mother murdering two of her own children is rarer again.

The habit worth building is simple: whenever you hear "the odds of this happening by chance are tiny", ask "compared with what?"
ideas.deep_dive:
The fallacy turns on a piece of probability that is easy to state and hard to feel. The chance of seeing this evidence if the person is innocent is not the same as the chance the person is innocent given this evidence. They only coincide if you ignore how rare the alternative is. The tool for getting it right is Bayes' theorem, which says you must weigh the likelihood of the evidence under each competing explanation, and also how plausible each explanation was to begin with.

Take the numbers from the most famous British case. Roy Meadow, a paediatrician, told Sally Clark's jury in 1999 that the chance of two cot deaths in an affluent, non-smoking family was about 1 in 73 million. He got there by taking a figure of roughly 1 in 8,500 for one such death and squaring it. That arithmetic assumes the deaths are independent, but cot death can run in families through shared genetic and environmental factors, so the true figure is higher. The Royal Statistical Society said there was no statistical basis for the number.

Then came the deeper mistake. Even if 1 in 73 million had been right, it describes how rare the deaths are. It does not say how likely it is that she was guilty. Double murder of babies is itself astronomically rare, and the jury needed to compare the two rarities, not hear only one.

The limit: this does not mean small probabilities are useless. It means they must always be set against the rival story. And in cases like these there is usually a prior question, whether any crime happened at all, that no probability can answer on its own.

examples.title: Sally Clark and the 73 million
examples.text: Sally Clark, a solicitor, lost two baby sons, in 1996 and 1998, and was convicted of murdering both in 1999. At trial, paediatrician Roy Meadow said the odds of two cot deaths in such a family were 1 in 73 million, a figure reached by squaring a single-death estimate of about 1 in 8,543. The Royal Statistical Society later criticised it. Her conviction was quashed by the Court of Appeal in January 2003 after it emerged that bacteriological evidence suggesting a natural death had not been disclosed. She had served more than three years and died in 2007.

examples.title: Lucia de Berk and 342 million
examples.text: Lucia de Berk, a Dutch nurse, was convicted in 2003 and 2004 of seven murders and three attempted murders, after deaths clustered on her shifts. A criminologist told the court the odds of this happening by chance were 1 in 342 million. The Royal Statistical Society later noted that, once real factors were allowed for, a cluster like it could be as likely as 1 in 25. The case was reopened in 2008 and she was cleared of all charges. The tiny number had done the work that evidence should have done.

Caveat: these were extreme cases where a wrong number was presented to a jury as near-proof. In ordinary life the fix is just to ask what the competing explanation is and how likely it is.
ideas.try_this: Next time you read "the odds of this being a coincidence are a million to one", write down the rival explanation and ask honestly how likely that is.

ideas.title: Zebra stripes are a fly repellent
ideas.idea:
The most likely reason zebras have stripes is not camouflage or cooling, but to keep biting flies off.

For over a century, people offered tidy explanations: stripes dazzle lions, shed heat, help zebras recognise each other. In 2014 a team led by Tim Caro at the University of California, Davis, tested five of these ideas against data from across Africa. Only one lined up. Where biting flies such as horseflies and tsetse were worst, the animals' stripes were boldest and covered the most of their bodies. Later experiments backed this up. Horses dressed in zebra-striped coats attracted fewer landing flies than plain ones, and in Japan, cows painted with stripes drew roughly half as many bites as unpainted cows.

It is a good reminder that a satisfying story is not evidence, and that evolution often solves ordinary problems, such as being bitten.
ideas.deep_dive:
The puzzle is old, and the popular answers sounded plausible: stripes confuse predators, cool the body, or signal identity. What was missing was a direct, comparative test.

Caro and colleagues supplied one. They mapped the range and stripe pattern of the zebra species and their relatives, and set them against environmental variables, including temperature, habitat and the breeding conditions for tabanid flies (horseflies), tsetse and other biters. They found no consistent support for camouflage, predator avoidance, heat management or social interaction. The one factor that matched was the biting-fly hypothesis: stripe intensity was strongest where the flies were thickest.

Then came experiments on the how. When researchers watched horseflies approach captive zebras and domestic horses, the flies had trouble landing on the stripes. Dressing horses in striped coats had a similar effect. Biting flies also carry diseases such as trypanosomiasis, so avoiding bites is a real evolutionary advantage.

The limits matter. The cow trial used only six animals. A later study found sharply contrasting stripes deterred flies while faint ones did not, found no evidence that polarised light was the key, and a 2024 review notes how stripes work is still poorly understood. The fly explanation looks strong, but it is not the final word.

examples.title: A continent-wide comparison
examples.text: In 2014, Tim Caro's team at UC Davis published "The function of zebra stripes" in Nature Communications. They compared stripe patterns across zebras, horses and asses against five hypotheses: camouflage, predator avoidance, heat management, social function and fly avoidance. Stripes were most extensive where horseflies, tsetse and other biting flies were most troublesome, and there was no consistent support for any other explanation. Because the horsefly distribution wasn't mapped directly, they used the best breeding conditions for those flies as a stand-in.

examples.title: Painting cows in Japan
examples.text: In 2019, Tomoki Kojima and colleagues in Japan painted six Japanese Black cows in a Latin-square design: black-and-white stripes, black stripes only, or nothing. The black-and-white striped cows attracted significantly fewer biting flies than either of the others, roughly half as many in press coverage, and they showed fewer fly-repelling behaviours like head throws, ear beats and tail flicks. The authors saw it as a possible way to protect cattle without pesticides, though the trial was small and only a first step.

examples.title: Horses in zebra coats
examples.text: Caro and Martin How went further, watching horseflies as they tried to land on captive zebras and domestic horses, and testing horses dressed in zebra-striped coats. The flies repeatedly failed to land on the striped coats. A later study found that sharply contrasting stripes deterred flies while faintly contrasting ones did not. For a farmer or rider the practical lesson is real: bold contrast seems to disrupt a fly's landing, though exactly why is still being researched.

images.caption: Plains zebras in Maputo National Park, Mozambique. The bold stripes may matter less for predators than for the flies that bite them.
images.credit: Charlesjsharp / CC BY-SA, via Wikimedia Commons

why: Evidence: Caro et al. (Nature Communications, 2014) compared five hypotheses across species; field and cow experiments since then point the same way.
Caveat: the experimental samples are small, and how the stripes actually put flies off is still not understood. 'Biting flies' is the best-supported explanation, not a closed case.
ideas.try_this: Think of a 'just so' story you accept without evidence, about your work or your family. What would a direct test of it look like?

ideas.title: Everyone privately disagrees, and nobody says so
ideas.idea:
Groups can follow a norm that almost nobody privately believes in, because each person thinks everyone else does.

Psychologists call this pluralistic ignorance. Picture a lecture where the speaker asks if anyone is confused. Every hand stays down. Each student reads the stillness as proof that they alone are lost, so they keep quiet, and the silence confirms everyone else's reading. Nobody lies; everybody is misreading everybody. The effect is strongest where people judge others by behaviour (what they can see) while judging themselves by private feelings (what they can't).

In a classic study at Princeton, students were uneasy about the campus drinking culture but assumed the average student was comfortable with it. Left alone, that gap kept the culture going. A later study found that teaching students about this gap, in a peer-focused session, reduced their drinking.
ideas.deep_dive:
Much of the modern evidence comes from Deborah Prentice and Dale Miller at Princeton. In a 1993 paper in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, they surveyed students about drinking on campus. Each rated their own comfort with campus drinking habits, and their estimate of the average student's comfort, on a scale of 0 to 10. The students consistently believed they were more uncomfortable than the typical student. That cannot be true of everyone at once.

What made the finding matter was what the misperception did. In their longitudinal study, a random sample of 25 male and 25 female sophomores was phoned in September and again in December. Over those months, the men shifted their own attitudes towards what they wrongly thought was the norm. Women did not change their attitudes, but felt more alienated. Perceived deviance, though illusory, tracked with campus alienation.

The remedy is information. Schroeder and Prentice tested this in 1998. Students were told about pluralistic ignorance, either in a group discussion focused on peers or in a session aimed at the individual. Four to six months later, those in the peer-oriented condition reported drinking significantly less.

The limits: the samples were small, the data were self-reports, and critics argue some of the effect is people genuinely updating from what they see, or simple measurement error. It also depends on a norm being publicly visible but privately doubted, which is not always the case.

examples.title: The Princeton drinking study
examples.text: In 1993, Prentice and Miller phoned a random sample of 50 Princeton sophomores, 25 women and 25 men, in September and again in December. Students rated their own comfort with campus drinking and that of the typical student on a 0 to 10 scale. They saw themselves as less comfortable than their peers, an impossible result if everyone was right. Over the term, male students' attitudes drifted towards the imagined norm, while female students kept their private views but felt more alienated from campus life. Believing you are the odd one out had real costs.

examples.title: Telling students the truth
examples.text: In 1998, Schroeder and Prentice tried to fix it. Students in a peer-oriented condition discussed pluralistic ignorance as a group problem. Four to six months later they reported drinking significantly less than students given an individually focused version. It is a rare case where a psychological bias was tackled directly, with a follow-up. The intervention was cheap: one session, aimed at getting private opinions into the open.

why: Evidence: Prentice & Miller (JPSP, 1993), 50 Princeton sophomores surveyed twice; Schroeder & Prentice (1998) tested an intervention with follow-up after 4 to 6 months.
Caveat: small samples and self-reported behaviour; some critics think part of the effect is real information-based conformity. It works best where a norm is visible but privately doubted.
ideas.try_this: Next time a room goes quiet after 'any objections?', say what you privately think, or ask the question you suspect others share, and see how many nod.

ideas.title: A volcano gave us Frankenstein and the bicycle
ideas.idea:
A single eruption on an Indonesian island in 1815 helped shape a famous novel and, plausibly, a vehicle you still ride.

When Mount Tambora blew in April 1815, it threw an estimated 100 cubic kilometres of debris into the sky, the biggest eruption in recorded history. Its sulphur veil dimmed the sun across the northern hemisphere, and 1816 became "the year without a summer": cold, wet, with failed harvests and soaring food prices. Locked indoors beside Lake Geneva, a group of writers, Lord Byron, Mary Shelley and John Polidori among them, passed the time with a ghost-story contest. It produced Frankenstein, The Vampyre and Byron's poem Darkness. The same shortage of oats is often said to have set a German inventor, Karl Drais, thinking about transport that needed no horse.

The lesson is how far distant events ripple: the connections are partly plausible rather than proven, but they are real enough to learn from.
ideas.deep_dive:
Tambora, on the island of Sumbawa in what is now Indonesia, began erupting in April 1815 and rated 7 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index, the second-highest level. Its climactic blast around 10 April left a caldera about 6 km across and 1,100 m deep. Estimates of the human toll vary: roughly 10,000 deaths in the initial eruption, and up to 71,000 if the starvation and disease that followed are counted.

The global effect came from sulphur dioxide, which turns into tiny droplets high in the stratosphere and reflects sunlight. Average temperatures fell across the northern hemisphere in 1816. A 2019 study reported by CNN found that the cold summers of that year would not have happened without the eruption. In Europe and North America the result was crop failure, famine and food riots; the price of oats, which fed the horses that moved everything, rose sharply.

Historians are more cautious about the cultural links. The Villa Diodati gathering is well documented: on 16 June 1816, with bad weather keeping the party indoors, Byron proposed that each guest write a ghost story. Mary Shelley, then 18, began Frankenstein there. Polidori's The Vampyre and Byron's Darkness came out of the same summer. That the weather helped is clear; how much it mattered compared with the company and the reading of German horror stories is a judgement call.

The bicycle link is the shakiest. Drais is said to have been spurred by the lack of horse feed, and his first ride took place on 12 June 1817. Sources describe it as plausible and widely repeated, not settled.

examples.title: A summer that never came
examples.text: After Tambora, the northern hemisphere suffered a summer so cold that 1816 is remembered as the year without one. A 2019 study reported by CNN found that those cold summer temperatures wouldn't have been possible without the eruption. The cold and wet brought crop failures and famine across Europe and North America, and food prices soared. It was a climate shock with a single, identifiable cause on the other side of the world.

examples.title: Ghost stories at Lake Geneva
examples.text: In June 1816 Lord Byron rented the Villa Diodati near Geneva and hosted Percy and Mary Shelley, Claire Clairmont and John Polidori. Poor weather kept them indoors for days, and on 16 June Byron proposed that each write the scariest ghost story they could. Mary Shelley, then 18, began Frankenstein; Polidori wrote The Vampyre; Byron wrote the apocalyptic poem Darkness. Most accounts agree the gloomy weather shaped the mood, though how much is debated.

examples.title: Karl Drais and the running machine
examples.text: In 1817, the German inventor Karl Drais made the first recorded ride of his Laufmaschine, a wooden two-wheeler pushed along with the feet, from Mannheim towards Schwetzingen on 12 June. CNN and other accounts say that high oat prices after the cold harvest of 1816 helped inspire his search for transport that didn't depend on horses. The link is plausible rather than proven, and the machine itself did not catch on during his lifetime on the poor roads of the day.

why: Evidence: the Tambora eruption and the cold of 1816 are well documented; a 2019 study found the cool summers would not have occurred without it.
Caveat: the Frankenstein link is plausible and widely cited, and the bicycle link is the weakest, so treat them as likely contributing factors rather than sole causes.
ideas.try_this: Pick one thing in your life that seems purely local, and trace a distant event, such as a harvest or a price rise, that may have shaped it.

ideas.title: The trend that reverses when you split the data
ideas.idea:
A pattern in the combined numbers can disappear, or even flip, when you look inside the groups.

This is Simpson's paradox. In autumn 1973 the University of California, Berkeley admitted about 44 per cent of male graduate applicants but only about 35 per cent of female ones. It looked like clear bias against women. Yet when statisticians broke the figures down by department, women were admitted at equal or higher rates in most of them. The gap came from where people applied: women applied in greater numbers to the most competitive departments, which turned away most candidates of either sex, while many men applied to easier ones.

Neither number is false. The question is which comparison answers the question you are really asking, and that depends on understanding what is driving the groups, not on the arithmetic.
ideas.deep_dive:
The effect is named after the statistician Edward Simpson, who described it in 1951, although Karl Pearson and Udny Yule had noticed similar effects decades earlier. It happens whenever a hidden third factor affects both the groups you are comparing and the outcome you are measuring. If the groups are very unevenly spread across that factor, the pooled average can point the opposite way from every subgroup.

The Berkeley case comes from a 1975 paper in Science by Peter Bickel, Eugene Hammel and J. William O'Connell. In the 1973 data, 3,738 of 8,442 male applicants (44.3 per cent) were admitted, against 1,494 of 4,321 women (34.6 per cent). That gap was large enough to be statistically significant. But applicants were applying to departments, not to the university as a whole, and the departments differed hugely in how hard they were to enter. Women's applications were concentrated in the harder ones. Within departments, there was no significant disparity, and women did slightly better in most.

A medical version appeared in a 1986 study of kidney stone treatments. Open surgery did better than a newer keyhole method for both small and large stones, yet the newer method looked better overall, because it was used more on the easier, small-stone cases.

The limit is that splitting the data is not automatically correct either. You can split on the wrong variable and manufacture a false story. You need a causal picture of why the groups differ to decide which numbers to trust.

examples.title: Berkeley's graduate admissions, 1973
examples.text: In 1973 Berkeley received 8,442 male and 4,321 female graduate applications; 3,738 men (44.3 per cent) and 1,494 women (34.6 per cent) were admitted. Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell checked the figures department by department. Women applied disproportionately to departments that were hard to get into, and within departments the sexes did not differ significantly. The 1975 Science paper concluded the pooled figures reflected application patterns rather than bias in the admissions committees. The finding still leaves open why those patterns existed.

examples.title: Kidney stones and a better treatment that looked worse
examples.text: In a 1986 study, Charig and colleagues compared open surgery with percutaneous nephrolithotomy for kidney stones. Open surgery had the higher success rate for small stones and for large ones. Yet pooled together, the newer procedure appeared more successful. The reason, as secondary accounts explain, is that doctors tended to use the more difficult approach on the harder, larger-stone cases, which have lower success rates for any method. Judging by the totals alone would have favoured the wrong treatment.

ideas.title: We remember how it ended, not how long
ideas.idea:
We judge an experience by its most intense moment and its ending, and largely ignore how long it lasted.

Psychologists call this the peak-end rule, with a companion effect called duration neglect. In a 1993 experiment led by Daniel Kahneman, people held a hand in painfully cold water twice: once for 60 seconds, and once for those same 60 seconds followed by 30 more in which the water was slightly warmer. Logic says the second trial is plainly worse, since it contains all the pain of the first plus extra. Yet most people chose to repeat the longer one, because it ended on a gentler note.

The practical upshot is odd but useful. How an experience ends can shape how you remember it, and decide whether you do it again, so endings are worth designing.
ideas.deep_dive:
The finding comes from work by Daniel Kahneman and colleagues, including Barbara Fredrickson, Charles Schreiber and Donald Redelmeier, on the difference between the experiencing self and the remembering self. The experiencing self lives through each moment. The remembering self keeps the story, and the story is what we consult when we decide whether something was good.

In the 1993 cold-water study, participants put a hand in water at 14 degrees Celsius for 60 seconds. In the other trial, the same 60 seconds was followed by 30 more seconds while the water warmed slightly to 15 degrees. They were then asked which they would repeat. Most chose the longer trial. Memory had weighted the worst moment and the end, and let the duration drop out.

The real-world version came in medicine. In a 1996 paper in the journal Pain, Redelmeier and Kahneman compared patients' moment-by-moment ratings of two minimally invasive procedures with their later memories. Then, in 2003, Redelmeier, Katz and Kahneman ran a randomised trial of 682 colonoscopy patients. For half of them, the scope was left in place without moving for a short interval at the end, which produced mild discomfort instead of an abrupt finish. Those patients rated the whole procedure as significantly less unpleasant afterwards, despite having had slightly more total discomfort.

The limits: the studies used short, discrete episodes, so it is hard to say how far the effect stretches to long ones. It is a tendency in memory, not a law, and it does not mean the experiencing self's suffering is any less real.

examples.title: Ninety seconds beat sixty
examples.text: In the 1993 study by Kahneman, Fredrickson, Schreiber and Redelmeier, volunteers kept a hand in painfully cold water for 60 seconds at 14 degrees Celsius, then in a second trial for 60 seconds followed by 30 more as the water warmed to 15 degrees. Later, given the choice, most chose to repeat the longer trial, even though it contained all the discomfort of the shorter one and more. This is the founding experiment behind both the peak-end rule and duration neglect: the added half-minute improved the memory by worsening the experience.

examples.title: The colonoscopy trial
examples.text: In 2003 Donald Redelmeier, Joel Katz and Daniel Kahneman randomly assigned 682 colonoscopy patients to one of two groups. In one, the procedure ended as usual. In the other, the tip of the scope was left in the rectum for a short extra interval, a milder discomfort than the main procedure. Patients in the extended group rated the experience as significantly less unpleasant when they looked back on it. The study, published in Pain, suggests that how a medical procedure ends can alter how patients remember it, which could matter because memory shapes whether people agree to repeat a procedure.

examples.title: Vacations and concerts
examples.text: Kahneman uses the same logic in his TED talk, with vacations and a concert as illustrations: a painful episode is remembered as less painful if the pain tapers off than if it stops sharply at its height, even when the total pain is greater. Roger Ebert's essay on the talk recounts a symphony anecdote in which a bad ending seems to spoil the whole concert in memory, even though the listener enjoyed it while it lasted. The remembering self edits the story, and the ending carries disproportionate weight.

ideas.title: A slime mould designed Tokyo's rail network
ideas.idea:
A brainless yellow blob can find network designs as efficient as those engineers draw up, by overbuilding first and pruning later.

In 2010 a team led by Atsushi Tero at Hokkaido University placed oat flakes on a damp surface at positions matching the cities around Tokyo, then set a slime mould, Physarum polycephalum, loose at the spot for Tokyo itself. The organism first spread out in every direction, covering the space with a dense web of tubes. Then it thinned that web, keeping the thick tubes that carried the most food and letting the rest wither. The result resembled the real rail network, and when scored on efficiency, fault tolerance and cost, it did comparably well.

The design lesson is that growth and selection can substitute for foresight. Rather than planning one perfect network, you start with plenty of connections and let use decide which survive.
ideas.deep_dive:
Physarum polycephalum is a single giant cell with many nuclei, not a plant or a fungus, that spreads as a bright yellow network of tubes. It has no brain, yet it can link food sources efficiently, and reportedly find its way through a maze. The 2010 study asked whether it could do something harder: build a good network between many points at once.

Tero and colleagues placed oat flakes, which the mould likes, at locations that corresponded to the cities around Tokyo. Because the mould avoids bright light, they used light to represent obstacles like mountains and lakes. The mould began by filling the space densely, and then gradually thinned the network, strengthening the tubes that carried the most flow and abandoning the others. The final network was compared with the real Tokyo rail system on three measures: efficiency (short travel between points), fault tolerance (still working if a link is cut) and cost (total length). On those measures the mould's network was comparable to the engineered one.

The team also turned the mould's behaviour into a mathematical model, published in Science as 'Rules for biologically inspired adaptive network design'. The point was not to replace planners, but to show a decentralised rule, reinforce what is used and let the rest decay, can produce robust results.

The limits: the mould was solving a simplified map, without gradients, politics, existing land use or demand. It matched the rail network on the chosen measures, not on everything a planner cares about. It is a design principle, not a blueprint.

examples.title: Oat flakes for cities, light for mountains
examples.text: In the 2010 Science study, Atsushi Tero and colleagues set oat flakes on a wet surface where cities around Tokyo would be, and let the mould grow from the position of Tokyo. They shone light on areas to stand for mountains and lakes, which the mould avoids. It first filled the whole space, then thinned its network to the branches connecting the food. The authors reported that the network showed efficiency, fault tolerance and cost comparable to the real Tokyo rail system.

examples.title: Finding the shortest path through a maze
examples.text: The Tokyo study built on earlier work showing the same organism could solve simpler problems. As Discover Magazine described, the mould can find the most efficient way of linking scattered food sources, and it can find the shortest path through a maze. The Tokyo study asked whether the same organism could handle a far harder problem: linking many points at once, not just two.

ideas.title: Disasters need several small holes to line up
ideas.idea:
Serious accidents rarely come from one mistake; they come from several small weaknesses lining up.

The psychologist James Reason pictured it as slices of Swiss cheese. Every safeguard in a system, such as a procedure, an alarm or a second pair of eyes, is a slice, and every slice has holes. Most of the time a hole in one slice is covered by solid cheese in the next. Harm gets through only on the rare occasion when the holes in all the slices align. That changes how you prevent accidents. Blaming the last person who touched the problem misses the point, because the holes were there already. The better question is how to add slices and shrink holes.

The idea cuts both ways. It explains why a flight can run out of fuel at 41,000 feet, and why a simple surgical checklist can cut deaths.
ideas.deep_dive:
Reason developed the model from studies of major accidents and catastrophic system failures, which tended to show multiple smaller failures leading up to the final hazard. His framework distinguishes two kinds of hole. Active failures are the unsafe acts of people at the sharp end, such as a slip or a wrong decision. Latent conditions are weaknesses built into the system long before, like confusing procedures, poor design, fatigue or missing equipment. Latent conditions are the dangerous ones because they sit dormant, waiting for an active failure to meet them.

The practical consequence is a different view of blame. If the holes pre-exist, then punishing the person who finally triggers the accident leaves the holes in place for the next person. A safer system adds independent layers, so one failure is caught by the next, and fixes the latent weaknesses it finds.

That is what the World Health Organization's surgical safety checklist does. It adds a few quick, standard checks, such as confirming the patient and the site of operation, at key moments. In a study of eight hospitals in eight cities, by Haynes and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2009, the death rate fell from 1.5 per cent to 0.8 per cent after the checklist, and complications fell from 11 per cent to 7 per cent.

The limits: Reason's diagram is a metaphor, and a 2005 survey found safety professionals interpret its features quite differently. Checklists reduce errors but, as one review put it, alone will not prevent all of them.

examples.title: The Gimli Glider, 1983
examples.text: On 23 July 1983, Air Canada Flight 143, a new Boeing 767, lost both engines at 41,000 feet over Red Lake, Ontario, having been fuelled with far less than it needed. Several holes lined up. Fuel was converted from litres using a pounds-per-litre factor, in an aircraft that worked in kilograms. The fuel-quantity system was already faulty and the jet had been dispatched under the minimum equipment list, so the cockpit gauges were blank. The pilots glided to a closed air base at Gimli, Manitoba. All 69 people on board survived.

examples.title: The WHO surgical safety checklist
examples.text: In a study published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2009, researchers introduced a checklist in eight hospitals in eight cities, from rich and poor settings. They compared 3,733 patients before it with 3,955 after. The death rate after surgery fell from 1.5 per cent to 0.8 per cent, and inpatient complications fell from 11 per cent to 7 per cent, according to secondary coverage of the paper. A review applying Reason's model found the checklist effective at reducing wrong-site surgeries and other errors.

ideas.title: Odysseus tied himself to the mast
ideas.idea:
The wisest use of willpower is to arrange things so you won't need it.

In Homer's Odyssey, Odysseus wants to hear the Sirens, whose song lures sailors to their deaths. He plugs his crew's ears with wax, has himself tied to the mast, and orders them to ignore his pleas. He does not trust his future self, so he takes the choice away in advance. The Norwegian philosopher Jon Elster, in his 1979 book Ulysses and the Sirens, made this the paradigm of precommitment: a rational person who knows they are prone to weakness of will accepts a small, deliberate cost now to avoid a greater loss later.

The idea is humble rather than heroic. It treats your future self as a stranger with different appetites and designs for that, instead of hoping you'll simply be strong. It is also practical, as the studies of savings accounts and psychiatric directives below show.
ideas.deep_dive:
Elster's argument starts from a puzzle in rationality. People can plan well, yet fail to do what they planned when the moment comes, through weakness of will. One response is to push harder at the moment. Elster's is to act earlier, while you are calm: bind yourself so the later temptation is either impossible to act on or more costly. He calls this precommitment, or self-binding, and takes Odysseus as the standard case.

The approach appears in many forms. Elster's own ordinary examples include a smoker who announces an intention to quit so that relapse would be costlier. Economists have tested it. In 2006, Nava Ashraf, Dean Karlan and Wesley Yin ran a randomised trial of a commitment savings product, SEED, at a bank in the Philippines. Clients choosing it agreed not to touch their money until they reached a goal or date. Of 710 clients offered it, 202 (28.4 per cent) accepted. Women who said at the start that they favoured present over future consumption later described themselves as disciplined savers, which is what a successful rope looks like.

In medicine, the same logic led to self-binding directives, sometimes called Ulysses contracts. People with conditions that come and go, such as bipolar disorder, can agree in advance to be admitted and treated during a future crisis even if they refuse at the time. The Netherlands amended its law in 2008 to include them.

The limits are real. Critics worry about self-paternalism, about pressure during drafting, and about the difficulty of allowing for a genuine change of mind. Binding yourself is wise only when the future self's resistance is the very thing you distrust.

examples.title: A bank account you can't raid
examples.text: In the Philippines, researchers Nava Ashraf, Dean Karlan and Wesley Yin worked with Green Bank of Caraga to offer a commitment savings account. Savers could not withdraw until a goal or date they chose was reached. Of 710 clients randomly offered it, 202 (28.4 per cent) opened one. Women who said at the start that they favoured present over future consumption later described themselves as disciplined savers. The study is the standard test of whether people knowingly tie their own hands, and some do.

examples.title: Ulysses contracts in psychiatry
examples.text: In mental health care, a self-binding directive lets a person who knows their capacity fluctuates agree in advance to hospital admission and treatment in a future crisis. The Netherlands added a self-binding paragraph to its Compulsory Admissions Act in 2008. Critics point to self-paternalism, undue influence during drafting, and the impossibility of accommodating a change of mind, so legal status varies across countries, and commentators note some of these contracts are not intended to be legally binding. It is the Odysseus story turned into law.

why: Evidence: Elster's philosophical account (1979) plus a randomised field trial of 710 offered clients (Ashraf, Karlan & Yin, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2006), and legal practice such as Dutch law since 2008.
Caveat: binding yourself costs flexibility and can fail if your circumstances change; the ethics of self-binding in psychiatry are contested.
ideas.try_this: Name one temptation you reliably lose to, and make it harder tonight, not tomorrow: delete the app, move the biscuits, schedule the transfer on payday.

ideas.title: Praise followed by decline is often luck
ideas.idea:
When something extreme happens, such as a brilliant performance or a dreadful one, the next attempt will usually be less extreme, even if nothing at all has changed. That drift back towards the average is called regression to the mean, and it quietly fools almost everyone.

It works because most results are skill plus luck. An exceptional result usually has an exceptional slice of luck in it, and luck doesn't repeat on demand. So the cadet who flew beautifully today will, on average, fly a little worse tomorrow, and the one who flew badly will do a little better.

The trap is the story we tell. If you praised the good flight and the next one was worse, praise seems to backfire. If you shouted at the bad flight and the next one was better, shouting seems to work. Both conclusions can be completely wrong, because the same pattern appears with no feedback whatsoever.

Whenever you see a change after an extreme result, ask first what would have happened anyway.
ideas.deep_dive:
The idea starts with Francis Galton. In the 1880s he compared the heights of adult children with those of their parents, using the average of the two parents (the "mid-parent"), after scaling women's heights up by 1.08. Children of very tall parents were tall, but on average less tall than their parents; children of very short parents were short, but taller than theirs. Galton put the ratio at roughly two to three: a child's deviation from the average was about two-thirds of the mid-parent's. He called it "regression towards mediocrity", which is where the word "regression" in statistics comes from. It is a statistical effect, not a genetic law: select anything for being extreme on one measurement and the next, imperfectly related measurement will sit closer to the middle.

Daniel Kahneman, in Thinking, Fast and Slow, told how a flight instructor in the Israeli Air Force said praise made cadets worse and shouting made them better. Kahneman saw that the instructor's observation was accurate but his explanation was wrong, and demonstrated it by having instructors toss coins at a target twice: the best first-time tossers did worse, the worst did better.

How strongly results regress depends on how much luck is involved. The less reliably one measurement predicts the next, the stronger the pull to the average. For something like height, it's modest; for a golf round or a quarter's sales, it can be large.

Where it stops applying: it isn't a force that drags people to mediocrity, and genuine change can happen on top of it. The skill is separating the two, usually by comparing with a group that didn't get the intervention.

examples.title: Kahneman's flight instructors
examples.text: In his account in Thinking, Fast and Slow, Kahneman describes a lecture to Israeli Air Force flight instructors about the value of praise. One senior instructor objected: when he praised a cadet for a clean manoeuvre, the next attempt was usually worse, and when he screamed at a cadet for a bad one, the next try was usually better. Kahneman explained that this is what you'd expect from chance alone, since an exceptional flight is likely to be followed by an ordinary one. To make the point, he had instructors toss coins at a target twice. The best first-time tossers did worse the second time and the worst improved, with no feedback involved.

examples.title: Speed cameras at accident black spots
examples.text: Cameras tend to be put where crashes have recently clustered, which is exactly where a run of bad luck would also make crashes fall afterwards. A 2008 study in the Journal of Safety Research looked at mobile cameras in Norfolk, England, and reported crashes down about 19% and fatal and serious crashes down about 44% at camera sites. A later commentary in the same journal argued the regression-to-the-mean adjustment had been miscalculated and underestimated, and the original authors agreed their conclusion needed amending. Careful camera studies now use control sites to separate the real effect from regression.

examples.title: The Sports Illustrated cover jinx
examples.text: Athletes who make the cover of Sports Illustrated often have a worse spell afterwards, which gave rise to a 'jinx' legend. The usual explanation is statistical: you only reach the cover after an unusually strong run, which generally includes a good dose of luck, so the next stretch tends to look weaker. Discover magazine treats it as a variation on regression to the mean, and the Wikipedia entry on the jinx gives the same account. It's an everyday case anyone who follows sport will recognise, and a reminder that a drop after a peak is the default, not evidence of a curse.

why: Evidence: Galton's 1880s height data, plus a century of statistics; the flight-instructor story comes from Kahneman's own telling and is a teaching anecdote, not a controlled study.
Caveat: regression explains only part of any change. Real effects exist, and the cure is a comparison group, not assuming everything is luck.
ideas.try_this: Think of something you changed after a bad run (a routine, a tool, a tactic) and credited for the recovery. What would you have expected to happen anyway?

ideas.title: A crowd's average can beat the experts
ideas.idea:
At a livestock fair in the west of England, around 800 people paid to guess the weight of an ox after it had been slaughtered and dressed. Francis Galton, who disliked the idea that ordinary people could judge anything well, collected the tickets. The middle guess was 1,207 lb. The real weight was 1,198 lb, a miss of under one per cent.

The lesson is that when many people estimate independently, their individual errors point in different directions and largely cancel out. What's left is the useful information they share. A crowd doesn't need to be clever, only varied and independent.

That second condition is the catch. Once people see one another's guesses, or defer to a loud voice, their errors line up instead of cancelling, and the crowd can be worse than a lone individual.

So the practical rule is simple: if you want a good estimate, collect several independent opinions before anyone discusses them, then take the middle value. Compare before you confer.
ideas.deep_dive:
Galton described the contest in a short note called "Vox Populi" in Nature in 1907. Visitors to a livestock show paid to guess the weight of an ox, and Galton obtained the tickets afterwards and analysed them. Counts of the entries vary slightly in accounts (about 787 usable tickets, roughly 800 overall), and a later check of his notes found small arithmetic slips in his own summary, but the main result is robust: the median guess, which he called the middlemost estimate, was 1,207 lb against an actual dressed weight of 1,198 lb.

The mechanism is statistical rather than mystical. Each guess is the truth plus an error. If the errors are unbiased and independent, they average towards zero as the group grows. Using the median, as Galton did, also stops a few wild guesses from dragging the answer.

The conditions matter more than the headline. Diversity of information helps, and so does independence. A well-known experiment by Lorenz and colleagues, published in PNAS in 2011, found that when participants could see others' estimates, the group's diversity shrank and the crowd's accuracy suffered, even while people felt more confident. Biases that everyone shares don't cancel either: a crowd asked to guess something it systematically misjudges will be confidently wrong together.

It stops applying whenever the question needs specialist knowledge nobody in the crowd has. Averaging a thousand people's guesses at a surgical dose won't help. It shines on estimation problems, such as quantities, dates and probabilities, where each person holds a scrap of relevant knowledge.

examples.title: Galton's ox
examples.text: At a livestock show in the west of England, visitors paid to guess the weight of an ox once slaughtered and dressed. Galton gathered the tickets and found the median guess was 1,207 lb. The butchered ox weighed 1,198 lb. He reported this in Nature in 1907 under the title 'Vox Populi'. Later analyses of his notes disagree slightly on the number of entries, from about 787 usable tickets to roughly 800, but all agree on the near-perfect median. It's the founding case for the idea, and it came from a man who had expected the crowd to do badly.

examples.title: Lorenz's experiment on social influence
examples.text: In a 2011 PNAS study, Jan Lorenz and colleagues had people estimate facts and let some of them see others' estimates before revising their own. Secondary accounts of the study report that the group's range of answers narrowed under social influence, which damaged the benefit of averaging, even though individuals grew more confident. The finding is a useful warning for meetings: if the boss speaks first, or the group discusses before anyone writes anything down, you lose most of the crowd's advantage. Collect private estimates first, then compare.

why: Evidence: Galton's single 1907 data set is real but a one-off; the independence requirement is supported by later experiments such as Lorenz et al. (2011).
Caveat: crowds fail on questions needing specialist knowledge and when everyone shares the same bias.
ideas.try_this: Before your next team decision, ask each person to write down an estimate (a date, a cost, a probability) privately, then compare the median with the loudest opinion.

ideas.title: Islands shrink giants and enlarge mice
ideas.idea:
On islands, big animals tend to get smaller and small animals tend to get bigger. Elephants end up the size of a pony; rodents grow to the size of a small dog. This is known as the island rule, after the biologist J. Bristol Foster, who set it out in the 1960s.

The logic runs on resources and risk. A large animal on a small island runs out of food sooner, so the individuals that need less food leave more offspring, and over many generations the species shrinks. A small animal, freed from the predators of the mainland, can afford to be bigger, which helps it survive scarce food and compete with its own kind.

On Sicily, an extinct dwarf elephant stood about a metre at the shoulder, a few per cent of the weight of its mainland ancestor. On Crete, a rodent grew at least eight times the size of its ancestor.

It is a tendency, not a law. Many species ignore it, and some famous cases turn out to have other explanations.
ideas.deep_dive:
Foster's 1964 work compared island mammals with their mainland relatives and found a pattern: small species such as rodents tended to grow, while large ones such as elephants and deer tended to shrink. Van Valen developed it further in 1973, and it became known as the island rule. A 2007 paper in Biology Letters traced the idea to these two and noted that exceptions have been reported, with some species or whole orders failing to conform.

The leading explanation is about energy and ecology. On a small island, food is limited and big predators are usually absent. Large animals gain from being smaller because they need less energy, and the pressure from competing with their own kind on limited land pushes towards smaller bodies. Small animals gain from being bigger when predators vanish, because larger bodies are better at storing fat, defending territory and surviving lean seasons.

The Mediterranean offers some of the best evidence because fossils are abundant. Sicily and Malta held at least three dwarf elephants; the Sicilian Palaeoloxodon falconeri stood about a metre tall. Crete's giant rodent Kritimys catreus was at least eight times heavier than its ancestor. On Flores in Indonesia, a dwarf Stegodon (a relative of elephants) lived before a larger species replaced it.

Where it stops applying: the rule is statistical, and a number of cases are disputed. The Galápagos giant tortoises, for example, need a different explanation. The hobbit of Flores, Homo floresiensis, is often cited as an island dwarf, but whether it fits is still argued.

examples.title: Sicily's one-metre elephants
examples.text: Sicily and Malta yielded the remains of at least three dwarf elephants, though reviews say the picture is complicated. The best known on Sicily, Palaeoloxodon falconeri, stood around one metre at the shoulder and weighed only a few per cent of its mainland ancestor. The animals were cut off on islands with limited food and no large predators. A bone-for-bone comparison with the ancestor shows how thoroughly evolution can shrink a species when resources are scarce.

examples.title: Crete's giant rodent
examples.text: The other half of the rule shows up in rodents. Kritimys catreus, an extinct rodent of Crete, was at least eight times the size of its ancestor. Freed from many mainland predators and competitors, small animals on islands often grow larger. Reports on island giants, such as those summarised by Reuters-based coverage in the Jakarta Post, pair the Cretan rodent with other cases to show the same trend running in reverse.

examples.title: The Wrangel Island mammoth correction
examples.text: For years the last mammoths, which lived on Russia's Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago, were described as dwarfs. A 1993 report argued that their teeth were small. Later work, including studies co-authored by Vartanyan himself, found the Holocene Wrangel mammoths stood about 180 to 230 cm at the shoulder, comparable to northern Siberian mammoths, and long-bone measurements in 2008 matched mainland animals. They were small, but not dwarfed. It's a good reminder that even a famous island story can be revised by better measurements.

why: Evidence: Foster (1964) and Van Valen (1973), with strong fossil support from Mediterranean islands.
Caveat: many species don't conform, and flagship cases such as the Wrangel mammoths and the Flores hominin have been revised or remain disputed.
ideas.try_this: Next time you see an 'obvious' evolutionary rule stated confidently, ask what the exceptions are and who has measured them.

ideas.title: Say when and where, and you will
ideas.idea:
Good intentions fail mostly at the moment of action, not at the moment of deciding. A simple fix is to turn "I will do X" into "If situation Y happens, then I will do X." Psychologists call this an implementation intention, and the idea was developed by Peter Gollwitzer.

The difference is specificity. "I'll get a flu jab" is a wish. "I'll get my flu jab on Thursday at 10am" is a plan with a cue. When the cue arrives, the action is triggered more or less automatically, instead of depending on you remembering and finding the motivation at that moment.

A large meta-analysis of 94 tests found that forming these if-then plans had a medium-to-large effect on whether people reached their goals. Field studies back it up: asking people to write down a date and time for a flu vaccination raised take-up, and helping voters plan how they'd vote increased turnout.

The plan works best for a clear, single action you already want to do. It won't create motivation you don't have.
ideas.deep_dive:
The concept comes from Peter Gollwitzer, who distinguished two kinds of intention. A goal intention states what you want ("I want to exercise more"). An implementation intention adds the where, when and how ("When I get home on Monday, I'll put on my trainers before I sit down"). By linking a specific situation to a specific response, you hand part of the work to the environment. When the cue appears, the plan is cued, rather than relying on conscious effort.

In 2006 Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran published a meta-analysis in Advances in Experimental Social Psychology. It combined 94 independent tests from 63 reports and found an average effect of d = 0.65 on goal attainment, a medium-to-large effect. That is a statistical effect size, not a 65 per cent improvement. A 2024 follow-up by Sheeran, Listrom and Gollwitzer reportedly covers 642 tests, so the newer estimate is the one to look for.

The field studies are the most convincing. In the flu study by Katherine Milkman and colleagues (PNAS, 2011), a firm's employees were mailed a prompt to write down their planned vaccination date and time. The control rate was 33.1%; asking for the date alone made little difference, while asking for date and time raised take-up by 4.2 percentage points. In Nickerson and Rogers (2010, Psychological Science), phone calls that helped voters plan when, where and how they would vote raised turnout by 4.1 points among those reached.

Where it stops applying: plans help with intentions you already hold. They struggle when the goal itself is vague, when the situation is unpredictable, or when you don't want to do the thing.

examples.title: Flu jabs at a large company
examples.text: Milkman, Beshears, Choi, Laibson and Madrian ran a field experiment at a large firm that offered free on-site flu clinics. Some employees got a mailing with a prompt to write down the date they planned to be vaccinated; others were asked to write down date and time. About 33.1% of the control group were vaccinated. Writing down the date alone raised take-up by 1.5 points, which was not statistically significant. Writing down date and time raised it by 4.2 points, which was. The result was published in PNAS in 2011.

examples.title: A voting plan on the phone
examples.text: Before the 2008 US election, David Nickerson and Todd Rogers randomised more than 287,000 people to different phone scripts. A standard encouragement call did nothing measurable, but a script that asked people when, where and how they'd vote raised turnout by 4.1 percentage points among those reached. The effect was concentrated in single-voter households, where turnout rose by 9.1 points, while households with several voters were unaffected, possibly because they already talk about voting. Sources disagree on which 2008 election (the primary or the general), so check the paper for detail.

examples.title: The 94-study review
examples.text: Gollwitzer and Sheeran's 2006 meta-analysis pooled 94 independent tests from 63 reports of if-then planning, covering goals from exercising to avoiding unwanted habits. The average effect on goal attainment was d = 0.65. The authors also reported benefits at several stages of pursuing a goal: starting, protecting an activity from interruption, and dropping a plan that isn't working. It's the evidence base to quote, though newer meta-analyses have since appeared.

why: Evidence: a 94-test meta-analysis (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006) plus large randomised field trials on flu vaccination and voting.
Caveat: real-world effects are a few percentage points, not dramatic, and they work only for goals you already want.
ideas.try_this: Pick one thing you keep meaning to do and write: 'When [specific time/place cue], I will [one concrete action].' Put it in your calendar.

ideas.title: Design a society without knowing your place
ideas.idea:
Imagine you must choose the rules of a society, but you won't know whether you'll be born rich or poor, healthy or ill, talented or not. What rules would you pick? That is the veil of ignorance, the thought experiment at the centre of John Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971).

Rawls argued that behind the veil, nobody could tailor rules to their own advantage, so the rules that emerge are fair by construction. He thought people would protect the worst-off position, since it might be theirs.

The device is useful beyond politics. Any time you're setting a rule for others, such as how to split a bonus, set a policy or divide chores, you can ask: would I accept this if I didn't know which seat I'd get?

It also reveals a real disagreement. Rawls said you'd protect the worst case. The economist John Harsanyi, who used a similar device earlier, said you'd maximise the average. Experiments suggest most people want something in between.
ideas.deep_dive:
Rawls's argument in A Theory of Justice asks us to imagine representatives in an "original position" who choose principles of justice behind a veil that hides their class, talents, gender and even their own idea of the good life. Because nobody knows where they'll land, Rawls claimed they'd choose principles that are fair to all. He argued for equal basic liberties, fair equality of opportunity, and the difference principle: inequalities are acceptable only if they benefit the worst-off.

A key point is the decision rule. Rawls denied the people behind the veil any knowledge of probabilities about which position they'd occupy, which pushes them to a cautious maximin strategy: make the worst outcome as good as possible. John Harsanyi had used a similar idea in 1953, before Rawls, but told the contractors they'd have an equal chance of being anyone, which leads to maximising the average welfare. The dispute between these decision rules is still live. Critics such as Nozick argued maximin is risk aversion taken to an extreme.

Experiments add something. In 1987 Frohlich, Oppenheimer and Eavey ran groups of five students who ranked and debated four principles of distributive justice behind a veil-like set-up. Groups reached agreement every time, but none chose pure maximin. They overwhelmingly picked maximising average income subject to a guaranteed minimum. A later study by Jackson and Hill found little support for maximin too.

Where it stops applying: the veil is a tool for testing fairness, not a decision machine. It can't settle trade-offs between liberty and equality by itself, and it assumes you can strip away your biases, which is harder than it sounds.

examples.title: Students choosing a distribution
examples.text: Frohlich, Oppenheimer and Eavey's 1987 experiments put 34 groups of five university students behind a veil-like set-up. Each student ranked four principles, then groups deliberated and needed unanimity to pick one. Every group reached agreement, but none chose to maximise the income of the worst-off alone. They overwhelmingly settled on the highest average income combined with a floor below which no one fell. The authors concluded that people's ideas of justice are complex and don't reduce to a single rule.

examples.title: Harsanyi's equal-chance observer
examples.text: John Harsanyi proposed in 1953 an impartial observer who imagines having an equal chance of being any member of society, and who therefore favours the policy that maximises average utility. Rawls, by contrast, denied that the contractors know the odds of any position. Same device, different assumption about probabilities, different recommended society. Later philosophers have argued that neither standard utilitarianism nor prioritarianism follows unless people are insensitive to ambiguity. It's the cleanest demonstration that the veil doesn't give one answer.

why: Evidence: a canonical philosophical argument, tested lab-style by Frohlich et al. (1987) with student groups; small, artificial samples.
Caveat: experiments favoured an average-with-floor rule rather than Rawls's strict worst-off priority, and the veil can't remove all bias.
ideas.try_this: Think of a rule you set or follow at work or home. Would you still choose it if you were randomly assigned a role in it, including the least advantaged one?

ideas.title: Your product will copy your org chart
ideas.idea:
Organisations that design systems tend to produce designs that mirror their own communication structure. This is Conway's law, from the programmer Melvin Conway in 1968. If four teams build a compiler, you will probably get a four-stage compiler.

The reason is practical. Interfaces between components get built where people have to negotiate across team boundaries, and the parts that need constant discussion end up inside one team. So the shape of the software follows the shape of who talks to whom, whether or not anyone intended it.

It matters because we usually think the other way round: we design the system, then assign people to it. Conway's law says the org chart is already designing the system for you.

The practical use is the "inverse Conway manoeuvre": if you want a particular architecture, shape the teams first. And if the product is awkward, look at where the teams meet.
ideas.deep_dive:
Melvin Conway wrote "How Do Committees Invent?" in 1967. Harvard Business Review rejected it, reportedly because he hadn't proved his thesis, and Datamation published it in April 1968. His claim was that any organisation that designs a system will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organisation's communication structure. Fred Brooks later named it Conway's law in The Mythical Man-Month.

The mechanism is simple. Early in a project the first decisions are about how to split the work, and that split determines who must talk to whom. Interfaces form where people don't talk easily; tightly coupled parts form where they do. Later changes to the design have to fight the existing communication paths.

For a long time the claim was folklore. In 2008 Nachiappan Nagappan, Brendan Murphy and Victor Basili published an empirical study of Windows Vista at Microsoft. They built metrics for organisational complexity, such as how many engineers touched a component and how scattered ownership was, and found these predicted failure-proneness better than traditional measures like code churn, complexity and dependencies.

In Conway's own anecdote, a research group of eight people building COBOL and ALGOL compilers split five and three, and the COBOL compiler ended up with more phases than the ALGOL one. Summaries disagree on the exact pass counts, so check his paper at melconway.com.

Where it stops applying: it describes a strong tendency, not a law of nature. Teams can deliberately reorganise, and small groups with fast communication can break the pattern.

examples.title: Windows Vista's organisation and bugs
examples.text: At Microsoft, Nagappan, Murphy and Basili studied how Windows Vista's organisational structure related to post-release failures. Their organisational metrics were statistically significant predictors of failure-proneness, and the precision and recall for finding failure-prone binaries were significantly higher than with traditional metrics such as code churn, complexity, coverage, dependencies and pre-release bugs. They framed it as testing Brooks's claim that product quality depends on organisation structure, a claim that had little empirical support until then.

examples.title: Conway's two compilers
examples.text: Conway's own illustration involved a contract research group of eight people asked to build both a COBOL and an ALGOL compiler. The group split roughly five and three. According to summaries of his paper, the COBOL compiler, built by the larger team, ended up with more passes than the ALGOL one. Treat the exact figures with some caution, since the sources I could check cut off before confirming the pass counts, but the shape of the story is consistent: the software mirrored the team sizes and how the work was divided.

why: Evidence: Conway's 1968 argument plus an empirical Microsoft study of Windows Vista (2008).
Caveat: the Vista result shows correlation between organisation and failures, and the original compiler story is anecdotal.
ideas.try_this: Draw your team's communication lines on paper next to the product's main components. Where do they match, and where is the product awkward because two teams meet?

ideas.title: Great discoveries tend to arrive in pairs
ideas.idea:
Inventions and discoveries that look like flashes of individual genius very often turn up in several places at once. The sociologist Robert Merton called these "multiples" and argued in 1963 that they are the normal pattern in science, not the exception.

Newton and Leibniz both developed calculus. Priestley and Scheele both isolated oxygen in the 1770s. Darwin and Wallace both reached natural selection. Elisha Gray filed a telephone patent the same day as Alexander Graham Bell.

The explanation is that ideas become reachable at particular moments. Once the earlier pieces exist (the right mathematics, better instruments, a certain body of data), several capable people are standing at the same frontier, and one of them will step over it soon.

That doesn't make individuals irrelevant. It means timing and groundwork matter at least as much as talent, and that if you notice the ingredients coming together, someone else probably has too. Speed and sharing are then the advantage.
ideas.deep_dive:
Merton's 1963 essay "Multiple Discoveries as Strategic Research Site" developed the argument that multiples may be the common pattern in science. He suggested that discoveries are, in principle, multiples, and that the ones that look singular are often multiples that were never completed or noticed. A sociology of science has a hard time with the "lone genius" story as a result.

The pattern appears on many scales. Calculus is the standard example: the mathematics that made it possible already existed, so the discovery would probably have occurred even without Newton's written work. Oxygen was found by Scheele and Priestley around 1774, quickly after studies of air showed it to be a mixture of gases and after better scales were invented. The telephone is a famous patent race, with Elisha Gray unaware of Bell's specifics yet filing on the same day.

The cleanest case may be evolution. In February 1858 Alfred Russel Wallace, ill with fever on Ternate, wrote an essay on natural selection and sent it to Darwin. Darwin passed it to Lyell and Hooker, who arranged for it to be read, alongside extracts from Darwin's writings, at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858. Neither man attended. Lyell and Hooker's introduction described them as having independently, and unknown to one another, conceived the same theory.

Where it stops applying: priority disputes can be bitter, and independent discovery isn't always as simultaneous as the stories make it sound. Stories of coincidence sometimes hide that one party saw the other's work or letters first.

examples.title: Darwin, Wallace and the Linnean Society
examples.text: In February 1858, Wallace wrote an essay on natural selection while ill at Ternate and sent it to Darwin, who had been working on the same theory for years. Lyell and Hooker arranged a joint presentation at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858, reading Wallace's essay alongside an extract of Darwin's earlier essay and his 1857 letter to Asa Gray. Neither man was present. The papers were published on 20 August 1858, with an introduction saying they had conceived the theory independently and unknown to one another.

examples.title: Calculus: Newton and Leibniz
examples.text: Newton and Leibniz are the textbook case of simultaneous discovery. Sources on Merton's work note that the mathematical ground for calculus already existed, which is why the discovery would very probably have occurred even without Newton's written work. The case shows how ideas can be waiting in the available pieces, and also how bitter the priority fight can become when two capable people reach the same place.

examples.title: Oxygen and the telephone
examples.text: Scheele and Priestley are credited with isolating oxygen independently, with the date given as 1774. One source ties the timing to earlier studies showing air is a mixture and to the invention of advanced scales. For the telephone, Elisha Gray, unacquainted with the specifics of Bell's work, filed a patent on the same day Bell did. Both examples show a discovery becoming reachable once surrounding tools and knowledge arrive.

why: Evidence: Merton's 1963 essay on multiples and numerous well-documented cases.
Caveat: some famous 'simultaneous' cases are muddied by priority disputes and shared sources.
ideas.try_this: Pick a project you're proud of that you think nobody else could have thought of. Who else had the same ingredients, and what would you do differently if you knew they were close?

ideas.title: The chemistry that feeds half of us
ideas.idea:
In 1909 Fritz Haber showed in a laboratory that nitrogen from the air could be combined with hydrogen to make ammonia. Carl Bosch scaled it up at the chemical company BASF, and by 9 September 1913 the world's first Haber-Bosch ammonia plant was producing at Oppau, in Germany.

It matters because plants need fixed nitrogen, and for most of history farmers relied on manure, legumes and imported guano or nitrate. Ammonia synthesis made fertiliser from air and energy. The historian-scientist Vaclav Smil argued that nearly half the world would go hungry without it, and that population could not have grown from 1.6 billion in 1900 to six billion without it.

The same chemistry made explosives. A century on, researchers writing in Nature Geoscience called it central to modern life, with benefits (food) and costs (war, and nitrogen pollution of rivers and seas).

Few inventions show so clearly that one technology can be both life-saving and deadly.
ideas.deep_dive:
Before Haber and Bosch, the supply of fixed nitrogen was a strategic problem. Crops need it, and nitrate came from limited natural deposits. Haber, a German chemist, patented his method in 1908 and demonstrated it in the lab in 1909. The practical challenge was making it work at industrial scale under high pressure and temperature, which was Bosch's contribution at BASF. Commercial production began at Oppau on 9 September 1913, just over four years after Haber's demonstration.

The scale of the effect is why Smil's argument gets cited so often. His 1999 essay in Nature argued that without ammonia there would be no inorganic fertilisers and nearly half of humanity would go hungry. Other estimates differ. A 2008 review in Nature Geoscience by Erisman and colleagues reports that around 2000, roughly 40% of the world's population depended on fertiliser inputs for food, and notes that the number is hard to pin down because of changes in crop varieties, mechanisation and breeding.

The history has a dark side. Ammonia is also the feedstock for explosives, and the review links Haber-Bosch nitrogen with millions of deaths in conflict. Haber himself championed chlorine gas as a weapon, overseeing its development before the attack at Ypres on 22 April 1915, and he still received the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for ammonia synthesis. The environmental cost, such as reduced biodiversity and algal blooms from nitrogen runoff, is also documented.

Where the story stops: "feeds half the world" is a rough estimate, not a measured figure, and yields also depend on seeds, irrigation and machinery.

examples.title: Oppau, 1913: the first plant
examples.text: BASF's own history records that the world's first Haber-Bosch ammonia plant started operating in 1913 at its new Oppau works north of Ludwigshafen. A Nature article dates commercial production to 9 September 1913, four years and two months after Haber's lab demonstration. The speed of that scale-up, carried out by Carl Bosch's engineers, is part of why the process changed agriculture within a generation.

examples.title: The Oppau explosion, 1921
examples.text: On 21 September 1921 at 7:32am, blasting intended to loosen hardened fertiliser in a silo at Oppau ended in a catastrophic explosion. The silo held about 4,500 tonnes of ammonium sulphate nitrate. BASF's history says more than 500 people were killed, and a German school text gives 561 dead and over 2,000 injured. BASF stopped producing that fertiliser and did not resume until 1940, with a modified process. It's a sobering example of how a food technology carries industrial risk.

examples.title: Haber's chlorine and Nobel Prize
examples.text: Haber also championed chlorine gas as a weapon, supervising the technology at his institute. A Norwegian encyclopedia reports that 167 tonnes of chlorine were released against British and French troops near Ypres on 22 April 1915, with limited tactical result because German troops did not follow up. In 1918 he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for ammonia synthesis. The pairing of the two facts is why historians still argue about how to judge him.

why: Evidence: BASF's records, Smil's essay in Nature (1999) and the 2008 Erisman et al. review in Nature Geoscience.
Caveat: 'half the world' is an estimate; figures range from about 40% to nearly half depending on method.
ideas.try_this: Next time you eat bread or rice, trace one step back: where did the nitrogen in that plant come from? What would the same field have yielded without it?
