ideas.title: The doctor ignored for saving mothers
ideas.idea:
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis, a young doctor at Vienna's General Hospital, noticed that women giving birth in the clinic staffed by doctors and medical students died far more often than those in the midwives' clinic. He suspected something carried from the autopsy room on the doctors' hands.

He ordered handwashing in chlorinated lime solution. In April 1847 mortality in the doctors' clinic was around 18%. By June it was about 2%.

His colleagues largely refused to accept it. Semmelweis had no theory of germs to offer, only a pattern, and it implied that doctors were killing patients. He died in 1865, shortly after being committed to an asylum. Germ theory and Lister's antiseptic surgery later vindicated him.

The "Semmelweis reflex" is the habit of rejecting evidence because it clashes with what we believe. It shows that being right about the data isn't enough; how a finding threatens people matters too.
ideas.deep_dive:
Vienna's General Hospital had two obstetric clinics. In the First Clinic, doctors and students delivered babies; in the Second, midwives did. Mortality from childbed fever was much higher in the First. Semmelweis tried and rejected many explanations, and concluded that "cadaverous particles" were carried by examining hands from the dissecting room to the labour ward.

In May 1847 he required handwashing in chlorinated lime. One account gives the April 1847 monthly rate as 18.3%, and the June rate as 2.2%, with July 1.2% and August 1.9%. Other accounts quote different baselines (a multi-year First Clinic average near 10% against under 4% in the Second), so the exact numbers depend on the period. The Second Clinic acted as a rough control, with unchanged practice.

His mechanism was wrong in detail. He picked chlorinated lime partly because it removed the smell of dead tissue; disinfection properties weren't yet known. Germ theory, developed by Pasteur and others, supplied an explanation, and Joseph Lister began applying carbolic acid to wounds around 1865. Semmelweis was committed to an asylum in 1865 at age 47 and died two weeks later from an infected wound, according to one account.

Where the story needs care: some popular retellings overstate things, for example that he "invented germ theory", which he did not. The "Semmelweis reflex" label came later and is a shorthand, not a rigorous psychological finding.

examples.title: Two clinics in Vienna
examples.text: Semmelweis's natural experiment compared the doctors' First Clinic with the midwives' Second Clinic at the Vienna General Hospital. Doctors' wards had roughly three times the mortality of the midwives' wards. After he introduced handwashing with chlorinated lime in mid-May 1847, monthly mortality in the First Clinic fell from 18.3% in April to 2.2% in June, according to a table reproduced from Wikipedia, and sources describe it as a drop of about 90%. The Second Clinic, where nothing changed, served as the comparison.

examples.title: Lister's carbolic acid
examples.text: Around 1865 Joseph Lister began applying carbolic acid to wound dressings, drawing on Pasteur's research on microbes. A BMJ piece notes that neither in Vienna nor in Glasgow did the new ideas meet with approval at first. Like Semmelweis, Lister had to wait. His approach eventually became standard surgical practice as germ theory took hold, showing that the same practical insight can win acceptance once a convincing explanation is available.

examples.title: The asylum and aftermath
examples.text: Semmelweis's ideas were rejected in his lifetime. One account says he was committed to a mental asylum in 1865 at age 47 and died two weeks later from an infected wound. His reputation recovered decades later as Pasteur's work and Lister's antisepsis explained what he had observed. The story is why 'Semmelweis reflex' has become shorthand for rejecting evidence that contradicts established belief.

why: Evidence: hospital mortality records from Vienna, with a rough natural control in the Second Clinic.
Caveat: baselines vary by source, his own explanation was wrong, and the popular version simplifies his motives and fate.
ideas.try_this: Recall the last time evidence challenged something you or your team do. What was your first reaction, and what would you have said if the messenger were someone you trusted?

ideas.title: We adapt less than we expect
ideas.idea:
We tend to assume a big change, good or bad, will set our happiness permanently higher or lower. Mostly it doesn't. People adjust, and their mood drifts back towards where it was. This is hedonic adaptation.

The classic study, from Brickman, Coates and Janoff-Bulman in 1978, compared 22 Illinois lottery winners with 22 controls and 29 people who had been paralysed in accidents. Winners were not noticeably happier than the controls, and the paralysed group, though less happy, was less so than most people would predict.

But the story is often told too neatly. Dan Gilbert acknowledged that he had overstated it: the groups were not equally happy. And later large panel studies suggest that some events, such as long-term disability, divorce and unemployment, leave lasting marks.

So the useful version is more modest: we over-predict how much a purchase or a promotion will change us, and under-predict how well we cope with setbacks. Enjoy good things deliberately, because the glow fades.
ideas.deep_dive:
The 1978 study by Philip Brickman, Dan Coates and Ronnie Janoff-Bulman is the origin of the lottery-winner story. It used small samples: 22 winners, 22 controls and 29 accident victims who were paralysed. Mean happiness ratings were 3.82 for the controls and 4.00 for the winners, a small difference, and 2.96 for the paralysed group.

The study's reputation exceeded its evidence. Dan Gilbert later acknowledged that he had misstated the results, saying that the groups were not equally happy and that the findings were weak, although the point about adaptation has been supported by later research.

The stronger evidence comes from long-running panel studies that follow the same people through life events. Richard Lucas, using the German Socio-Economic Panel and the British Household Panel, argued in a 2007 paper that long-term disability is associated with lasting changes in subjective wellbeing, and in a related review that divorced and unemployed people, on average, do not return to their previous happiness. Other researchers using German data found adaptation for working-age men, so the picture is not settled.

The takeaway is about forecasting. We tend to focus on the change and ignore how much of daily life stays the same, and we underestimate how much we will adjust. Where it stops applying: adaptation is partial and depends on the event. Some losses and some chronic conditions don't fade.

examples.title: The Illinois lottery study
examples.text: Brickman, Coates and Janoff-Bulman interviewed 22 Illinois lottery winners, 22 people from the same area as controls, and 29 people paralysed in accidents. Winners averaged 4.00 on a happiness scale against 3.82 for controls, and the paralysed group averaged 2.96. The authors read this as evidence of adaptation. Later commentary, including from Gilbert, points out the groups weren't equally happy and that the samples were small, so it's best treated as a suggestive early study, not proof.

examples.title: Lucas and the national panels
examples.text: Richard Lucas followed people through life events in two nationally representative longitudinal surveys: the German Socio-Economic Panel and the British Household Panel. His 2007 paper in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology concluded that long-term disability is associated with lasting changes in wellbeing. A related review argued that people who divorce or become unemployed do not, on average, return to their earlier happiness. Pagán-Rodríguez, using German data on working-age men, reported that adaptation does occur, so researchers still disagree on how complete it is.

why: Evidence: the 1978 lottery study (small samples, since criticised) plus later panel studies following thousands of people.
Caveat: adaptation is partial and varies by event; disability, divorce and unemployment appear to leave lasting effects in some studies.
ideas.try_this: Name one thing you were sure would make you happier and now barely notice. What could you do this week to notice it again on purpose?
